analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after childbirth.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House health subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required any health plan offering maternity coverage to pay for a minimum hospital stay after birth: 48 hours after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section. Plans could cover a shorter home-based visit instead if the mother chose it or her doctor found it medically necessary, and plans could not penalize a mother for choosing less care. It also required plans to tell enrollees in writing what the law guaranteed them.
analysis.who_benefits: Mothers and newborns, who in the mid-1990s were often discharged within 24 hours of delivery as insurers pushed for shorter stays. The bill guaranteed them time in the hospital to recover and for the baby to be monitored, with the choice of a covered home visit instead if they preferred.

how_it_helps.text: The bill required health plans that cover maternity care to pay for a minimum of 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section, for both mother and newborn [S3].

It included an exception allowing coverage of home post-delivery care instead of the hospital stay when the mother requests it or the attending physician finds inpatient care medically unnecessary [S3].
It barred plans from changing the terms of coverage based on an enrollee's choice of less than the minimum stay, so a mother who chose to leave early would not lose other benefits [S3].
It required plans to prominently notify every enrollee in writing about the required coverage, under rules set by the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor health plans, who would pay for the longer hospital stays, likely through higher premiums. Hospitals would receive payment for additional inpatient days.

drawbacks.text: A coverage mandate raises costs: plans and employers would bear the expense of the added hospital days, and those costs would tend to show up in premiums, a cost that falls partly on the workers and families the bill aims to help [S3].

The bill applies broadly to nearly any arrangement that pays health benefits, with a long list of exclusions but a wide general reach, so the mandate would touch many kinds of coverage rather than being narrowly targeted [S3].

A one-size-fits-all minimum stay overrides individual medical judgment in the other direction too, paying for hospital days some mothers would not have chosen if a covered home-care alternative were not already built into the requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and specific: newborns and mothers no longer rushed out of the hospital within a day of delivery, which was the common practice this bill targeted. The cost is a modest, spread-out one: higher premiums and employer plan costs. It is a fairly standard insurance mandate of the kind Congress itself later embraced in this area. The bill's weakness is less its design than its breadth; it applies to nearly all health-benefit arrangements. On balance, the benefit to mothers and infants outweighs the added premium cost, though the cost is real and would not vanish.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the bill on June 28, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S5].
On July 10, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where no further action was taken [S5].
The bill drew 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats and 1 Independent) but never advanced out of committee during the 104th Congress [S4].
The sponsor's introductory remarks were printed in the Congressional Record on July 11, 1996, a year after introduction, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who fund health plans were better off, avoiding the cost of a mandated 48- and 96-hour covered stay for another two years. Mothers and newborns, who were the bill's intended beneficiaries, got nothing.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and kept the record alive with introductory remarks a year after referral.

for.name: 11 of 435 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (10 Democrats and 1 Independent).

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for action; it was referred to the health subcommittee and stayed there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split appears in the record; the sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents [S4].

industries.note: The bill forces plans to pay for a minimum 48- and 96-hour post-delivery stay, ending the cost-saving practice of discharging mothers within about 24 hours. Its defeat preserved that practice and the insurers' ability to set shorter covered stays.
Guaranteed minimum stays mean additional covered inpatient days and more paid obstetric and newborn care. Longer stays also serve the medical interest of mothers and babies.
Plan sponsors would bear most of the mandate's cost through higher premiums, though many employees they cover are the same families who benefit from the guaranteed stays.
